item.title: After One-Click Video: The Inflow of Service-Type Content, the Failure of the Recommendation Pool Mechanism, and the BoLe System
item.description:
Institution: Bread Studio | Authors: Bo Zou, Chao Xu

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract AI-generated video tools shift content production toward service-type material, unbalancing the industry and overwhelming recommendation systems, prompting a dual-judgment BoLe framework to protect work-type content. Generated by thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small

Abstract

Generated by thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small In September 2026, a new large language model was released. Soon after, a new way of making explainer videos became very popular: people asked the model to write a program, and the program produced the video. "One-click video" content then appeared in large amounts on many platforms. On the surface, this is a rise in creative power at the level of the individual. We argue that, at a deeper level, it changes the structure of the content industry. This judgment rests on two observations. First, this wave of content is service-type content. People watch it to meet a need, not to enjoy the content itself. The other kind is work-type content. AI makes both kinds faster to produce. But anyone can come in and make service-type content, while work-type content is limited by the number of people who have something to say. So the ratio between the two slowly becomes unbalanced. Second, free platforms choose content through layers of trial viewing, and this uses up user attention. The total amount of attention is fixed. The unbalanced ratio also dilutes good content. A simplified mathematical model shows that, as long as these conditions hold, the recommendation pool mechanism will fail once new content grows past a certain multiple. Based on this, we discuss one possible way out. Machines and entry rules judge whether service-type content passes the bar. Trusted people judge work-type content. We call this the BoLe system. At the end, we briefly imagine how the two kinds of content may develop from here.

item.title: IntReal: A Real-World Dataset and Benchmark for Multimodal Interleaved Generation
item.description:
Institution: Nanjing University | Authors: Shaohan Yu, Jie Qin, Wende Tan, Haiwen Diao, Limeng Qiao

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract IntReal introduces a real-world interleaved multimodal dataset and evaluation framework to diagnose unified model strengths and improve generation through targeted training. Generated by thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small

Abstract

Generated by thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small Humans routinely consume multimodal content, where textual and visual information is naturally interleaved. Although Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) can jointly generate text and images, multimodal interleaved generation remains largely underexplored. Progress in this area is hindered by two key limitations: (1) the lack of well-defined interleaved generation tasks and corresponding training data, and (2) the absence of fine-grained evaluation protocols that can reliably diagnose model performance across different capability dimensions. To this end, we present IntReal, comprising two complementary components: IntReal-100K, a real-world dataset of multimodal interleaved samples spanning four major categories, and the IntReal Evaluation Suite, which evaluates model performance across seven complementary dimensions using specialized expert models, enabling coarse-to-fine diagnosis. Extensive experiments validate our evaluation suite through low inter-metric redundancy (max pairwise absolute Spearman's ρleq 0.42 ), high agreement with human judgments (83.3% accuracy), and strong consistency across different expert evaluators (Spearman's ρ> 0.9 ), supporting the complementarity and reliability of our metrics. By benchmarking four families of UMMs, we show that IntReal Evaluation Suite reveals distinct strengths and weaknesses across models. Post-training experiments demonstrate the utility of IntReal-100K for improving interleaved generation and further show that training unimodal generation can also benefit interleaved generation. These findings suggest that interleaved generation can benefit from modality-specific optimization, rather than requiring joint text-image training at every stage.

item.title: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments
item.description:
Authors: Tianci Xie, Zikun Cai, Chaoyun Zhang, Pinxue Guo, Bingxuan Li

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract WebAnything automates the reconstruction of reusable, source-grounded web environments from real URLs, enabling scalable agent training and evaluation with verified fidelity. Generated by thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small

Abstract

Generated by thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable website environments for reproducible training and evaluation. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities. We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization. An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture. We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks. Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor, WebAnything achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity metrics, with 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a blind audit. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by 6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness. Code: https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Web-Anything

item.title: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training
item.description:
Institution: IQuest | Authors: Ziyang Zeng, Tingyang Chen, Jia Deng, Qiyao Wang, Shuo Tang

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract WorkFactory builds coherent professional tasks via information planning and repair, yielding WorkPilot models that improve expert-level agent performance across benchmarks. Generated by thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small

Abstract

Generated by thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small Scaling supervised training for working agents requires diverse professional tasks that yield reliable expert demonstrations. However, missing or inconsistent task information can obstruct teacher execution and weaken the resulting supervision. We propose WorkFactory, a scalable framework for constructing coherent and executable professional tasks. Starting from professional intents, information-level planning builds an information support graph to guide task instantiation, explicitly representing the dependencies and locations of information required for the intended outputs. Probe executions then identify support failures and guide repairs while preserving the intended work. We construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and use the collected teacher trajectories to fine-tune Qwen models at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales, yielding the WorkPilot family. All three models improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B improving from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1. Scaling analyses reveal model-dependent diminishing returns, with execution length first increasing and then decreasing. Controlled component analyses show that planning and repair reduce probe-diagnosed task environment defects and improve downstream performance. The data and models are available at https://github.com/IQuestLab/WorkFactory.

item.title: VibeGame: Prompt-to-Game Development with AI-Native Engine and Self-Evolving Adversarial Agent Team
item.description:
Institution: Nanjing University | Authors: Wenbo Hu, Ken Li, Jiazhe Wei, Yukang Cao, Weiyi Hong

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract VibeGame is a framework that uses specialized adversarial agents and an AI-native engine to build complete 2D games from natural-language prompts with interactive validation and self-evolving reusable components. Generated by thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small

Abstract

Generated by thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small Large language model agents have enabled software development through natural-language interaction, but extending this paradigm to end-to-end game development remains challenging. Building a playable game requires coordinating code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, while allowing developers to validate their integrated behavior through interactive testing. We introduce VibeGame, a framework for creating complete 2D game projects from natural-language prompts and optional reference images. Its AI-native game engine represents project state as schema-validated structured text and provides frame-synchronous runtime control, enabling agents to inspect game states, execute actions, and verify behavior at their own pace. Built upon this interface, we design an Adversarial Agent Team of eight specialized agents to separate implementation from review, so that problems are found and fixed through multi-round loops. For each conducted and accepted project, we further introduce a training-free self-evolution mechanism to distill it into reusable skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts for future development. We evaluate prompt-assets-to-game (PA2G), where agents are given an asset library, and prompt-to-game (P2G), where agents generate their own art. On a GameCraft-Bench subset, VibeGame in P2G consistently outperforms a range of agent harnesses in either P2G or PA2G with the same underlying model, including GPT-6.1-Sol.
